abstract.title: Abstract
abstract.p: Recent evidence suggests that type I interferon (IFN‐I) signalling extends beyond its canonical roles in antiviral defence and immunomodulation. Over the past decade, dysregulated IFN‐I signalling has been linked to genetic disorders and neurodegenerative diseases, where it may contribute to neurological impairments. Microglia have emerged as key mediators of IFN‐I responses in the central nervous system. A distinct transcriptional state responsive to interferons has recently been identified in microglia. The activation of the IFN‐I pathway in these cells is now recognised as pivotal in both development and neurodegeneration. This review is divided into two main sections: the first examines the broader role of IFN‐I signalling in the central nervous system, particularly its contribution to neurological dysfunction; the second focuses on the specific state of interferon‐responsive microglia, exploring its mechanisms and relevance in neurodegenerative conditions. Finally, we discuss how these areas intersect and their implications for both healthy and diseased states.

sec.p: Keywords: brain, interferon‐responsive microglia, microglia, neuroinflammation, type‐I interferon

abstract.p: Recent insights reveal that type I interferon (IFN‐I) signalling plays critical roles in the nervous system beyond antiviral defence. Dysregulated IFN‐I activity is increasingly linked to neurological dysfunction and neurodegeneration, with microglia as central mediators. This review explores the broader impact of IFN‐I signalling on the nervous system and delves into the emerging transcriptional state of interferon‐responsive microglia (IRM), highlighting its relevance in development, disease, and potential therapeutic avenues.

sec.title: Interferon signalling in the central nervous system
IFN‐I in antiviral immunity and its impact on cognitive function
sec.p: IFN‐I consist of a group of small, inducible cytokines, such as IFNα and IFNβ, that drive the antiviral response in nonimmune cells and orchestrate the progression from innate to adaptive immune response upon viral infection [1, 2]. Viruses can introduce pathogen‐associated molecular patterns (PAMPs), which include proteins and nucleic acids, in host cells. These are recognised by pattern‐recognition receptors (PRRs) such as toll‐like receptors (TLRs) [3], retinoic acid‐inducible gene I (RIG‐I)‐like receptors (RLRs) [4], and cytosolic cyclic GMP‐AMP synthase (cGAS) [5, 6, 7]. PAMP binding to PRRs triggers the activation of interferon regulatory factors like IRF3 and IRF7, which bind to specific sequences in the promoter regions of IFN‐I genes, leading to their expression (Fig. 1). The secreted IFN‐I spreads and amplifies the response in surrounding cells. IFN‐I binds to its cognate receptor, the interferon alpha and beta receptor (IFNAR), activating the JAK/STAT pathway and leading to the transcription of a variety of interferon‐stimulated genes (ISGs) [8]. ISGs act in concert to restrict viral replication through nucleic acid degradation and inhibition of gene expression, protein synthesis, and virion assembly [9, 10, 11].

sec.p: While IFN‐I confers protection against viral infections, its activation in the central nervous system (CNS) presents a unique challenge. The CNS is safeguarded by a complex barrier system that helps exclude toxins and pathogens [12]. However, many neurotropic viruses, including herpesviruses and rabies virus, can breach these barriers and infect neural cells such as neurons, glial cells, and vascular cells, all of which can upregulate IFN‐I expression in response to various stimuli [13]. Although all CNS cell types are responsive to IFN‐I, each mounts a distinct response [13, 14, 15, 16]. Neurons, though highly sensitive to IFN‐I, produce little themselves, allowing them to activate antiviral pathways while minimising the risk of neuroinflammation [17, 18, 19]. In contrast, microglia and astrocytes serve as primary IFN‐I producers, with microglia showing a more extensive and diverse response to INFα stimulation [20, 21]. Oligodendrocytes, on the other hand, exhibit a more restrained IFN‐I response, producing lower levels of IFN‐I during viral infections and expressing fewer interferon‐stimulated genes compared to microglia [22]. While this immune response is essential for antiviral defence, a strong immune reaction can cause acute meningitis, encephalitis, and myelitis, which manifest with behavioural and cognitive impairments [23]. Due to its antiviral and immunomodulatory properties, IFNα has been used to treat chronic viral infections such as hepatitis C and herpes. However, IFNα therapy can result in side effects, including reversible depression and impaired cognition, resembling the mild subcortical dementia characteristic of viral encephalitis (e.g. human immunodeficiency virus‐associated encephalitis (HIVE)), and certain neurodegenerative disorders, such as Huntington's disease and Alzheimer's disease (AD) [24, 25, 26].

The recent coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID‐19) pandemic, caused by infection with SARS‐CoV‐2, has affected hundreds million people worldwide (https://www.worldometers.info/coronavirus/). Although COVID‐19 is a severe acute respiratory pathology, affected individuals can also develop a range of extrapulmonary manifestations, including neurological symptoms [27]. Persistent neurological symptoms such as brain fog, headaches, and memory issues have been observed in some patients recovering from the acute phase of COVID‐19 syndrome, raising concerns about the potential for chronic cognitive impairment associated with post‐COVID‐19 syndrome [28, 29]. Notably, long‐term cognitive sequelae have also been documented in other coronavirus syndromes caused by SARS‐CoV‐1 [30] and MERS‐CoV [31].

The mechanisms underlying cognitive impairment in post‐COVID‐19 and other postviral syndromes remain incompletely understood. Recent studies suggest that IFN‐I‐driven immune responses in the choroid plexus may contribute to cognitive dysfunction if unresolved in a timely manner [32]. Indeed, enhanced brain IFN signalling is a hallmark of COVID‐19 neuropathology [33] and is also a distinctive feature of human immunodeficiency virus‐associated dementia (HAD) [34, 35, 36]. Experimental evidence from a mouse model of HIVE demonstrated that treatment with an IFN‐I neutralising antibody reversed memory impairment [37]. At the cellular level, IFN‐I blockade reduced microgliosis and prevented dendritic loss in the brain of HIVE mice, whereas exogenous IFN‐I administration to primary neuron cultures induced a dose‐dependent loss of dendritic complexity [37]. Similar findings have emerged from models of vesicular stomatitis virus M2 (VSV‐M2) infection, where IFN‐I signalling at the brain's barriers has been linked to cognitive impairment. Infection with VSV‐M2 in adult mice resulted in significant behavioural and cognitive changes, comparable to those induced by recombinant IFNβ and classical IFN‐I triggers such as 3pRNA and poly(I:C) [16]. Using a regulatable intersectional gene inactivation model, Blank et al. demonstrated that mice lacking IFNAR1 specifically in brain endothelial and epithelial cells were protected from depressive‐like behaviour and learning and memory deficits induced by systemic VSV‐M2 infection. These findings implicate the choroid plexus as a key site where IFN‐I responses drive cognitive and behavioural changes following viral infections [16].

Taken together, the evidence suggests that dysregulated type I IFN signalling, particularly at the brain's barriers and within the choroid plexus, plays a critical role in cognitive impairment associated with postviral syndromes. These findings highlight IFN‐I as a potential therapeutic target for mitigating long‐term neurological consequences of viral infections.

sec.title: Beyond immunity: IFN‐I influences experience‐dependent brain function and behaviour
sec.p: IFN‐I signalling extends beyond antiviral defence and immunomodulation, playing a crucial role in homeostatic processes within the developing and adult CNS [38]. Transcriptomic analyses of macrophages and B cells from Ifnar1‐deficient mice have revealed a tonic IFN‐I activity under steady‐state conditions [8]. Neurons and astrocytes are also sensitive to basal IFN‐I levels, playing a key role in sustaining neural circuit homeostasis and function [39, 40].

Beyond its homeostatic role, IFN‐I signalling is dynamically regulated by experience. In mice, chronic stress modulates IFN‐I levels and contributes to the associated behavioural response [41]. Mice subjected to chronic unpredictable stress exhibit increased serum IFNβ levels, and systemic blockade of IFN‐I signalling attenuates stress‐induced deficits in social behaviour and spatial working memory [41]. Notably, chronic stress‐induced synapse loss and behavioural deficits are reversed in mice lacking IFNAR in adult microglia, highlighting a key role for microglia in mediating IFN‐dependent effects in response to stress [42].

Chronic stress is a major risk factor for neuropsychiatric disorders, and IFN‐I dysregulation has been implicated in their pathophysiology. Patients with major depressive disorder show upregulated interferon signalling [41, 43] and, as noted above, IFNα treatment frequently induces depressive symptoms, fatigue, anxiety, and cognitive disturbances [25]. Together, findings from both animal models and clinical studies suggest that variations in baseline IFN‐I levels influence brain function and behaviour through diverse mechanisms affecting neurons, microglia, and potentially other CNS cell types.

sec.title: Pathophysiological impact of IFN‐I overproduction in Interferonopathies, autoimmune and developmental disorders
sec.p: The dysregulation of IFN‐I signalling is not only implicated in stress‐related behavioural changes but is also a hallmark of several genetic and autoimmune disorders. A key example is type I interferonopathies, a group of inherited conditions caused by mutations in DNA‐ and RNA‐sensing pathways, which lead to chronic IFN‐I overproduction [44, 45, 46]. Up to 52 distinct mutant genotypes have been classified under this umbrella, with striking clinical similarities, particularly in brain and skin involvement [44, 46, 47, 48]. One of the most well‐characterised type I interferonopathies is Aicardi–Goutières syndrome (AGS; OMIM 225750) [48, 49, 50]. This inherited leukoencephalopathy is marked by elevated intrathecal and serum IFNα levels [51]. Although AGS presents with clinical heterogeneity, its classic severe form manifests in early infancy with psychomotor delay, feeding difficulties, irritability, aseptic febrile episodes, and chilblain skin lesions. Over time, the condition progresses to secondary microcephaly, brain atrophy, and spastic tetraparesis, stabilising thereafter. Most severe cases lead to death before the age of 10, whereas milder forms have a later onset and slower progression [50].

Animal models provide further insight into IFN‐I‐driven neuropathology. Genetically engineered mice with astrocyte‐specific IFNα overexpression (GIFN mice) exhibit a transgene‐dose‐dependent phenotype, characterised by progressive weight loss, inactivity, and ataxia, followed by severe seizures that often result in premature death [52, 53]. These mice also develop hallmark AGS‐like neuropathological features, including basal ganglia and cerebellar calcifications, meningoencephalitis, gliosis, and neurodegeneration, suggesting that sustained intrathecal IFNα overproduction is neurotoxic [52, 53]. However, the mechanisms underlying IFNα‐induced neurotoxicity remain poorly understood. Recent findings highlight cerebral endothelial cells and microglia as key responders to IFNα, with the cerebral microvasculature emerging as a central mediator of IFNα‐induced neurotoxicity in AGS [54]. These observations highlight the need for further investigation into the cellular and molecular pathways through which IFNα induces neuroinflammation, contributing not only to the neuropathological features of AGS but also to those of other type I interferonopathies.

Beyond interferonopathies, IFN‐I dysregulation also plays a pathogenic role in autoimmune disorders. Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is a chronic inflammatory disease of unknown cause that primarily affects the skin, joints, kidneys, and multiple organ systems, including the nervous system [55]. Notably, IFN‐I has been identified as a key pathogenic factor in SLE, and prolonged IFN‐I treatment has been linked to iatrogenic lupus [56, 57]. Neurological symptoms, particularly brain fog, are highly prevalent in lupus and are associated with deficits in concentration, attention, and memory [58]. However, the role of IFN‐I in these cognitive symptoms remains to be fully explored.

Another condition with IFN‐I hyperactivation is Down's syndrome (DS; OMIM 190685), a genetic disorder caused by trisomy 21, which is associated with intellectual disability, neurological complications, and increased autoimmune susceptibility [59]. The IFN pathway is consistently activated in individuals with trisomy 21, likely due to gene dosage effects, as four of the six IFN receptors (IFNAR1, IFNAR2, IFNGR2, and IL10RB) are encoded on chromosome 21 [60, 61, 62, 63, 64]. In multiple mouse models carrying triplicated Ifnr genes, IFN hyperactivity is a consistently observed across diverse brain regions and developmental stages [65]. Notably, normalising Ifnr copy number alleviates several hallmark features of DS, such as abnormalities in embryonic development, neuronal viability, immune hypersensitivity, septal heart defects, craniofacial malformations, and cognitive impairments [63, 66]. However, the exact cellular and molecular mechanisms underlying these alterations remain largely unknown. In iPSC‐derived organoid and chimeric mouse models of DS, microglia exhibit hyperactivated IFN signalling and enhanced synaptic pruning [67]. Knockdown of IFNAR in DS microglia restores normal synaptic pruning, suggesting that IFN‐mediated microglial activation contributes to neurodevelopmental alterations in DS [67]. These findings highlight the central role of IFN‐I signalling in DS pathophysiology and underscore the importance of further research to unravel the underlying mechanisms and therapeutic potential. In this context, JAK signalling pathway inhibitors may represent a promising strategy that could offer therapeutic benefits for individuals with DS [68].

Overall, these findings highlight the critical role of IFN‐I dysregulation in neurological dysfunction across diverse conditions, from genetic interferonopathies to autoimmune and developmental disorders. A deeper understanding of IFN‐I‐mediated mechanisms in the brain could pave the way for targeted therapeutic strategies to mitigate its detrimental effects.

sec.title: IFN‐I signalling in ageing and neurodegeneration
sec.p: There is growing evidence that enhanced interferon type I (IFN‐I) signalling contributes to cognitive decline associated with normal ageing and plays a role in cognitive impairment in neurodegenerative diseases [69, 70]. Specifically, transcriptomic analyses have consistently revealed a heightened IFN‐I response in the aged brain [71, 72, 73, 74], with the choroid plexus and microglia identified as primary sites of IFN‐I activation [71, 75, 76, 77]. Additionally, a significant proportion of other CNS‐resident cells, including astrocytes, oligodendrocytes, neurons, and endothelial cells, exhibit an IFN‐I‐dependent response during normal ageing [74]. Notably, pharmacological and genetic blockade of IFN‐I signalling can counteract age‐related cognitive decline and promote neuronal survival in aged mice [71, 74, 77, 78]. Conversely, chronic overexpression of IFNβ at the choroid plexus impairs hippocampus‐dependent spatial learning and memory abilities in adult mice [77]. These studies collectively highlight that increased IFN‐I signalling contributes to age‐associated cognitive decline [71, 74, 77, 78].

Emerging data suggest that microglia are key mediators of the detrimental effects of heightened IFN‐I activity on brain function [74, 77, 78]. Aged microglia display an IFN‐I response that can be reversed through pharmacological blockade of IFNAR [77]. Furthermore, selective ablation of the IFN‐I receptor, IFNAR1, in adult microglia reverses the interferon‐stimulated gene (ISG) signature observed in the cortex of aged mice [74]. Together, these findings suggest that microglia not only respond to local IFN‐I signals but also act as a major source of IFN‐I in the aged brain. The consequences of a heightened microglial IFN‐I response at the circuit and behavioural levels have been explored using gain‐ and loss‐of‐function approaches in mice [74, 77, 78]. Mice lacking IFNAR1 in adult microglia are protected from age‐associated neuronal loss in the hippocampus [74]. However, the role of microglia in mediating age‐related cognitive decline due to enhanced IFN‐I remains unclear. Interestingly, mice with selective ablation of IFNAR1 in microglia are resistant to learning and memory deficits induced by IFNβ overexpression at the choroid plexus in adulthood [77]. Conversely, mice with constitutive activation of IFN‐I signalling in microglia through the STING pathway exhibit impaired hippocampal‐dependent learning and memory, alongside a loss of hippocampal neuron density, mimicking the cognitive decline seen in aged mice [78]. Collectively, these findings suggest that enhanced IFN‐I signalling contributes to cognitive decline in normal ageing by impacting various CNS‐resident cells, with microglia likely playing a central role in mediating its detrimental effects.

There is also increasing evidence supporting the involvement of IFN‐I in major neurodegenerative diseases, including Alzheimer's disease (AD). AD patients exhibiting clinical dementia show a heightened IFN‐I gene signature in the parahippocampal gyrus, and activation of the IFN pathway is associated with disease progression [79]. More recent data further extend this observation, showing activation of the cGAS‐STING pathway in the brains of individuals with AD [80, 81]. Mouse models of brain amyloidosis or tauopathy also exhibit activation of the IFN‐I pathway [79, 80, 81, 82, 83, 84, 85]. Notably, pharmacological inhibition and genetic ablation of the IFN‐I pathway in experimental AD models ameliorate a wide range of AD hallmarks, including Aβ plaque pathology, synapse loss, neural plasticity impairment, and cognitive deficits [80, 81, 82, 83, 84, 86]. In contrast, enhancing the IFN‐I response in an AD model (5xFAD) exacerbates Aβ plaque burden and synapse loss [79, 84]. Overwhelming genetic and experimental evidence supports the role of microglia in the pathogenesis of AD [87], with growing data suggesting their pivotal role in driving the IFN‐I response in AD [80, 81, 82, 83, 84, 85, 88, 89]. Furthermore, a direct causal link between IFN‐I signalling in microglia and synaptic pathology in AD has been demonstrated in 5xFAD mice [82].

IFN‐I dysregulation has been also observed in experimental models of other neurodegenerative disorders, such as Parkinson's disease (PD) and prion disease [90, 91]. Mice lacking IFNAR1 show reduced progression of ME7 experimental prion disease, with diminished synaptic and neuronal loss and a delayed onset of neurological impairment [90]. Similarly, genetic ablation of STING protects against motor deficits, pathological α‐synuclein (α‐Syn) accumulation, and dopaminergic neuron loss in the α‐Syn preformed fibril (PFF) mouse model of PD [91]. Τhese findings highlight the IFN‐I signalling pathway as a shared feature among neurodegenerative diseases of distinct origins [92], suggesting that IFN signalling plays a significant role in driving disease progression.

Taken together, the findings suggest that IFN‐I functions within a specific range, crucial for maintaining homeostasis and proper brain function. Both the absence and excessive activation of the IFN‐I response can lead to brain dysfunction and, ultimately, neurodegeneration [93]. Additionally, there is compelling evidence that microglia play a central role in mediating the IFN‐I‐induced response within the CNS, while also serving as a significant source of interferon.

sec.title: Microglia in health and disease: Sentinels of the central nervous system
sec.p: Microglia are resident macrophages of the central nervous system [94, 95]. These cells originate from committed myeloid progenitors in the yolk sac and migrate into the neural tube during early embryonic development, around E8.5 in mice, spreading throughout the central nervous system [96, 97, 98, 99]. Microglia contribute to development, homeostasis, function, and repair of the neural tissue [100, 101, 102]. During neurodevelopment, they play critical roles in the establishment, wiring, and refinement of neural circuits [103, 104, 105, 106, 107, 108]. In the healthy adult brain, microglia act as sentinels, constantly remodelling their processes to monitor the surrounding environment and respond rapidly to changes [109, 110, 111]. To achieve this, microglia are equipped with a wide array of cellular receptors and proteins [112, 113]. They shape hippocampal adult neurogenesis [114], regulate neurovascular coupling [115], tune neuronal activity [116], drive experience‐dependent synaptic structural plasticity [117], and control behaviour [118, 119, 120]. Microglial responses are also key to host defence against infectious pathogens, and their activation is present in virtually all central nervous system pathologies, including neurodegenerative diseases, tumours, epilepsy, stroke, and trauma [121, 122, 123]. Dysregulated microglia and microglia‐driven neuroinflammation are hallmark features of both physiological and pathological brain ageing [101, 124, 125, 126, 127].

sec.title: Microglia heterogeneity
sec.p: It is tempting to surmise that the broad range of functions performed by microglia may be underpinned by a diverse array of phenotypes. Indeed, microglia are not a uniform population; rather, they exhibit significant heterogeneity that is region‐specific and regulated by developmental stages [113, 128]. The concept of microglial diversity has deep roots, first proposed in the original description of microglia by Rio‐Hortega, who identified ‘satellite’ microglia [94]. He also observed notable regional variation in the density and distribution of microglia throughout the nervous system [94]. In the early 1990s, Siamon Gordon's group used immunocytochemical detection of the macrophage‐specific plasma membrane glycoprotein F4/80 [129] to characterise microglial density across regions of the forebrain [130]. This study revealed that microglia account for 5–12% of the total cell population in the adult mouse forebrain [130]. Therefore, microglial density varies across brain regions, with areas such as the hippocampus, olfactory bulb, and basal ganglia being highly populated, moderately populated regions including the cortex, thalamus, and hypothalamus, and sparsely populated areas like fibre tracts, cerebellum, and brainstem [130].

In addition to regional differences in cell proportions, microglia exhibit significant morphological variation depending on their location. They range from rounded shapes in blood–brain barrier‐free regions to highly ramified cells with long processes throughout the neuropil, and even longitudinal branching in fibre tracts that align parallel to the longitudinal axis of nerve fibres [130]. Recent studies have extended these foundational observations, showing that microglia exist along a spectrum of functional states, each associated with brain region‐dependent phenotypic identities [76, 131, 132, 133].

Over recent years, significant progress has been made in understanding the local cues from the microenvironment and the genetic programs that govern and shape microglial phenotypic diversity and function, both in the developing and adult brain, as well as in disease contexts [112, 134, 135, 136, 137, 138, 139]. Early genomic studies revealed that microglia undergo distinct transcriptional stages throughout development [140, 141]. The advent of high‐throughput single‐cell transcriptomics has further illuminated the complexity of microglial phenotypic diversity. These studies show that during development, microglia exhibit extensive transcriptional heterogeneity, potentially linked to population expansion and local specification, as well as dynamic periods of neurogenesis and synaptic remodelling [142, 143, 144, 145]. This contrasts with the relatively uniform transcriptional profile observed in adult microglia [146, 147]. During ageing and disease, microglia undergo changes, acquiring a variety of molecular phenotypes and activating specific transcriptional programs in response to highly complex processes [138, 143, 148, 149, 150, 151, 152, 153, 154, 155, 156, 157] (Fig. 2). The interested reader is referred to several in‐depth reviews on this topic [158, 159, 160, 161, 162, 163, 164, 165, 166, 167]. This surge of discoveries has sparked growing interest in unravelling the variety of phenotypic states in response to environmental changes, including their dynamics and the mechanisms regulating transitions between different functional states. More importantly, a central question in the field is how the molecular diversity of microglia relates to specific functional states and whether these molecular phenotypes are linked to the broad spectrum of functions that microglia perform.

sec.title: Interferon‐responsive microglia in health and disease
sec.p: As mentioned earlier, microglia exhibit significant phenotypic diversity, with specific microglial states corresponding to different stages of development, ageing, and disease progression. One such distinct phenotype is interferon‐responsive microglia (IRM), which has been observed to play a critical role in both the ageing brain and various neurodegenerative diseases. The activation of the interferon response gene programme in microglia has been well documented in aged mouse brains [75, 76, 138] and in neurodegenerative conditions, both in animal models and human patients [138, 143, 148, 153, 154, 157, 168, 169, 170, 171, 172] (Fig. 3).

sec.p: Bart Eggen's group first described the activation of interferon signalling in aged microglia using gene expression microarrays to profile the transcriptome of bulk microglia isolated from aged mice and a mouse model of accelerated ageing (Ercc1Δ/KO) [75]. Later, McColl and colleagues extended these findings, identifying heightened type I interferon pathway activation in cerebellar microglia of young adult mice (4 months old) [76]. This response included the upregulation of transcriptional regulators of the interferon pathway (e.g. Irf7, Stat1, Stat4) and interferon‐stimulated genes encoding antiviral effector proteins (e.g. Ifit2, Ifitm3, Oas1). Interestingly, the interferon pathway in cerebellar microglia exhibited more pronounced age‐dependent regulation compared to telencephalic regions, such as the neocortex, hippocampus, and striatum [76]. The authors proposed that this heightened interferon activity in cerebellar microglia could be linked to a more immuno‐vigilant phenotype in the white matter‐enriched cerebellum and/or cerebellum‐specific, age‐dependent expression of endogenous retroviruses (ERV), such as murine leukaemia virus‐type ERVs (MuLV‐ERV) [76].

Early RNA‐seq profiling of microglia isolated from the postmortem right parietal cortex of adult subjects identified a gene expression signature characteristic of human microglia. Regulatory network analysis of this signature revealed a core set of transcriptional regulators, including key interferon pathway components such as TRIM22, MNDA, IRF1, IRF5, IRF7, and IFI16 [135]. Additionally, a meta‐analysis of expression profiles from purified microglia across various conditions confirmed interferon response activation in response to viruses, lipopolysaccharide (LPS), glioma, and neurodegenerative disease models, including AD models. This activation was particularly evident in microglia from aged mice and was more pronounced in cerebellar than cortical microglia [138]. More recent work from Wei Cao's laboratory demonstrated the presence of IFN‐I‐responsive microglia surrounding amyloid deposits in the brains of 5XFAD AD model mice [79, 82].

Single‐cell gene expression studies have further unveiled the transcriptomic heterogeneity of microglia, with a more pronounced diversity observed in development and disease states. One of the most consistently identified microglial subpopulations is IRM (Fig. 2), which is defined by the activation of a broad array of interferon‐stimulated genes (ISGs) (Fig. 4). A seminal study by Tsai and colleagues using the CK‐p25 inducible mouse model of severe neurodegeneration [173] identified reactive microglial phenotypes emerging at later disease stages, characterised by a co‐regulated module containing type I interferon response genes [148]. Notably, interferon response genes such as Isg15, Ifi30, Irf7, Oasl, and Ifitm3, which were induced in microglia from the CK‐p25 model, were also among the genes most significantly correlated with age in human microglia [135, 148]. Early single‐cell RNA sequencing (scRNA‐seq) studies provided limited coverage due to the low number of microglia profiled [174]. For instance, Tsai and colleagues analysed only 1685 high‐quality single microglia using plate‐based scRNA‐seq [148]. However, later studies significantly increased throughput. Sala‐Frigerio and colleagues, for example, profiled approximately 11 000 high‐quality microglia from the App
NL‐G‐F knock‐in AD mouse model [168]. Their analysis identified six major microglial subpopulations, including an IRM cluster with high expression levels of type I interferon pathway genes, such as Ifit2, Ifit3, Ifitm3, Irf7, and Oasl2 [168]. Interestingly, this study also found that IRM levels increased with age in both App
NL‐G‐F and wild‐type mice [168]. Subsequent scRNA‐seq data expanded the evidence for IRM presence in additional AD models [157, 169, 172] and in human AD patients [153, 154, 170]. IRM have also been identified in other neurodegenerative conditions, including ALS/FTD in C9orf72 mutant mice [171], an experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis model of multiple sclerosis (MS) [143], and glioma [175].

sec.p: Given the prevalence of IRM in neurodegenerative diseases, it is crucial to determine their role in disease pathology. Microglia are known to modulate amyloid pathology in AD by both promoting the formation and compaction of Aβ plaques [176, 177]. In AD models, ISG‐expressing microglia accumulate in an age‐dependent manner, surrounding nucleic acid‐containing Aβ plaques [79, 82]. IFN‐I signalling has been implicated in exacerbating amyloid pathology [80, 81, 82, 83, 84, 86]. Based on these findings, it has been hypothesised that IFN‐activated microglia may facilitate amyloid formation in neurons [82], potentially through IFITM3‐mediated activation of gamma‐secretase activity [178].

Beyond plaque modulation, IRM have also been implicated in aberrant synaptic remodelling in AD. IFN‐I‐activated microglia rapidly eliminate dendritic spines [79], and conditional deletion of Ifnar1 in microglia reduces synaptic engulfment in 5XFAD brains [82]. Similar findings have been reported in C9orf72−/− ALS/FTD mouse models, where interferon‐activated microglia promote excessive synaptic pruning, leading to premature synapse loss and exacerbated cognitive deficits [171]. Together, these data suggest that IRM contribute to neural network dysfunction in neurodegenerative diseases (Fig. 5). Further studies are needed to determine whether targeted inhibition of interferon signalling in microglia could mitigate cognitive decline in AD models.

sec.p: The advent of droplet‐based scRNA‐seq has enabled high‐throughput single‐cell transcriptomics, significantly advancing our understanding of microglial heterogeneity [179]. This technology has facilitated the identification of cell states present at low frequencies, including IRM. Pioneering work from Beth Stevens' laboratory revealed that IRM not only emerges in disease contexts but also accumulates with ageing [143], potentially contributing to the chronic inflammatory state of the aged brain [75, 76, 77, 78]. Subsequent studies confirmed the presence of IRM in aged mouse and human brains [78, 156, 170, 180], as well as in the adult brain under baseline conditions, albeit at low levels [147, 155]. Recent data also suggest a transient role for IRM in engulfing damaged neurons during central nervous system development [145]. Loss of IFN‐I signalling disrupts phagolysosomal function in microglia and leads to the accumulation of neurons with DNA damage, whereas IFN‐I gain of function enhances neuronal engulfment and modulates cortical excitatory neuron populations [145]. These findings indicate a potential physiological role for IRM in neural circuit remodelling (Fig. 5).

Taken together, these studies highlight the presence of IRM across various conditions, from normal ageing to neurodegenerative diseases. While IRM likely plays important roles in homeostasis and pathology, the molecular mechanisms governing their emergence and plasticity remain largely unexplored. Further research is needed to determine whether targeting IFN‐I signalling in microglia could provide therapeutic benefits in neurodegenerative diseases.

sec.title: Regulatory mechanisms governing IRM identity
sec.p: A key question is how IFN‐I activation is regulated in microglia. In AD, microglia and other cell types within the brain can respond to extracellular DNA, likely released from damaged neurons and associated with amyloid plaques. This DNA may act as a pathogen‐ or danger‐associated molecular pattern, triggering antiviral immunity [79, 82]. Additionally, IFN‐I induction in microglia can be elicited by cGAS‐STING pathway activation in response to cytosolic leakage of mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA), a process that occurs during ageing [78] and in neurodegenerative conditions due to pathogenic tau accumulation [81]. These factors likely coexist from the early stages of the disease, collectively driving IFN‐I pathway activation. In the aged brain, microglia may also respond to interferons released by other cell types, such as the choroid plexus [71].

Despite progress in understanding IFN‐I signalling in microglia, little is known about the master regulatory genes controlling IRM identity. Gene regulatory network analyses have highlighted canonical regulators of the IFN‐I pathway, such as IRF7 [148, 170]. Loss‐of‐function approaches have further identified key transcription factors involved in IFN‐I regulation. For instance, Matcovitch‐Natan and colleagues demonstrated that the transcription factor MafB negatively regulates IFN‐I signalling, maintaining microglia in a homeostatic state under normal conditions [140]. MafB‐deficient microglia exhibit strong upregulation of type I interferon antiviral responses, suggesting that MafB prevents inappropriate activation of antiviral pathways [140]. Mechanistically, MAFB interacts with IRF3, displacing the transcriptional coactivator CBP and thereby preventing the assembly of functional transcription preinitiation complexes [181]. Similarly, C9orf72 has been implicated in myeloid homeostasis [182, 183], with its loss leading to hyperactive IFN‐I production, which can be attenuated by STING inhibition [184]. Further studies have shown that C9orf72 deficiency intrinsically alters microglial transcriptional profiles, directly impacting IRM gene expression [171]. While these findings offer valuable insights, the regulatory mechanisms underlying IRM remain poorly understood, underscoring the need for further research into microglial plasticity and its molecular regulation.

As described above, single‐cell profiling has revealed a spectrum of microglial phenotypes. However, the extent to which these molecular phenotypes represent metastable states remains largely unknown. Moreover, little is understood about the dynamics of transitions between these states. Trajectory inference methods have been employed to infer microglial phenotypic transitions during development [145], across ageing [155], in experimental models of neurodegeneration [157], and in AD [153]. However, these approaches have provided only a limited understanding of microglial plasticity [145, 153, 155, 157]. In addition to intrinsic methodological constraints [185], microglial trajectory inference is further complicated by the overall molecular homogeneity of the population, the low frequency of minor states such as IRM, and the lack of clear intermediate states in the data. A deeper understanding of these transitions will require integrative approaches combining single‐cell genomics with functional studies to capture the dynamic nature of microglial states in health and disease.

sec.title: Conclusions and perspectives
sec.p: A growing body of evidence underscores that, beyond its antiviral response, IFN‐I plays a pivotal role in regulating CNS homeostasis and the development of various neurological diseases. These findings are fostering an increasing consensus on how variations in IFN‐I levels contribute to neurological disturbances observed in genetic conditions such as interferonopathies [45, 46, 47, 48], as well as autoimmune diseases like SLE [55, 56, 57]. However, further research is needed to clarify the mechanisms underlying neural circuit dysfunction and cognitive fog, which remain largely unexplored.

Dysregulated interferon signalling during ageing has been observed across species, from mice to humans [71, 75, 76, 77]. Data from murine genetic models suggest that interferon signalling significantly contributes to age‐related cognitive decline [71, 77, 78]. Exacerbated IFN‐I signalling is also implicated in more common neurodegenerative diseases, including PD [91] and AD [70]. Notably, antisense oligonucleotides targeting the IFNα receptor effectively reduce neuroinflammation, restore brain integrity, and reverse neuropathology in a mouse model of cerebral interferonopathy [186]. This offers a promising therapeutic strategy not only for these untreatable diseases but also for other pathologies involving dysregulated IFN‐I signalling, such as neurodegenerative disorders. Seminal data suggest that activation of the cGAS‐STING pathway, triggered by the release of DNA from damaged or dysfunctional mitochondria, may play a role in cognitive impairment associated with ageing and neurodegenerative diseases [187]. The preservation of cognitive abilities observed in preclinical models following pharmacological interventions that limit cGAS‐STING activation raises hope for the development of novel therapeutic strategies [65, 68]. However, it is essential to fully understand the side effects of prolonged pathway inhibition, particularly with regard to the body's defence against infections in these conditions [188]. An alternative approach could involve designing strategies to reduce cytosolic mtDNA levels, which increase with ageing and neurodegenerative diseases [78, 81]. Interestingly, recent findings show that stimulating mitophagy during ageing can improve mitochondrial function and reduce mtDNA‐mediated inflammation, alleviating age‐related neurological decline [189, 190].

A deeper understanding of the cellular and molecular mechanisms driving exacerbated IFN‐I responses in ageing and neurodegenerative diseases, as well as in other conditions like interferonopathies and SLE, is crucial for effective clinical translation. IRM microglia appear to play a significant role in structural plasticity defects and cognitive impairment observed in these conditions. However, the signalling mechanisms remain underexplored, and many questions persist. For instance, the relative contribution of microglia‐mediated direct (e.g. complement‐mediated synapse phagocytosis [104]) or indirect (e.g. through paracrine signalling to neurons, astrocytes and other cell types of the CNS) contributions to these processes is still unclear. It also remains unknown whether IRM may drive remodelling of other structures beyond synapses, such as the perineuronal nets surrounding parvalbumin interneurons [191, 192], and how this remodelling may contribute to pathology in specific contexts. The tissue location of IRM beyond AD, where they cluster around amyloid plaques [69, 70], is also largely unknown. Generating high‐quality brain maps of IRM locations in situ across life stages and conditions may inform their functional relevance. Furthermore, developing strategies to target the IRM state specifically will help clarify its contribution to disease progression. Conventional DNA delivery methods are inefficient in targeting microglia [193], but recent advancements have introduced novel tools that may enable effective in vivo manipulation of specific microglial populations [194, 195]. Gain‐ and loss‐of‐function approaches will be crucial for advancing our understanding of IRM functions across neurodevelopmental stages, adulthood, ageing, and disease conditions. These tools could also improve our understanding of the molecular mechanisms governing microglial plasticity and state dynamics, which remain poorly understood.

IRM microglia may emerge during early development, phagocytosing neurons with accumulated DNA damage and contributing to neural circuit remodelling during critical neurodevelopmental stages [145]. Initial data suggest a role for the RIG‐I‐MAVS pathway in this process [145], but whether the signals regulating this mechanism originate in neurons or microglia remains unclear [196, 197]. Further research is needed to explore how inflammatory processes, such as those caused by viral or bacterial infections during development, may contribute to the emergence of neuropsychiatric disorders such as autism.

In summary, while significant progress has been made in recent years in understanding the role of IFN‐I and IRM in CNS homeostasis and disease, many questions remain unanswered, and new ones have emerged. A comprehensive understanding of the roles of IFN‐I and IRM may enhance our knowledge of fundamental biological processes, such as neurodevelopment and the regulation of neural circuit homeostasis. Moreover, it could contribute to the development of new strategies to modulate the course of highly prevalent neurodegenerative diseases, such as Alzheimer's disease.
